case_info.scenario: A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

distractors: Bone metastases from submandibular gland cancer
case_info.caption: A, Sagittal T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging shows multiple hypointense lesions in the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. B, Sagittal computed tomography image (soft tissue window) demonstrates mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction.
case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.

[Clinician's statement]
Based on the histopathology and immunostaining profile—desmin positivity, CD99 positivity, ALK D5F3 positivity, and cyclin D1 positivity—this is consistent with an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT). The tumor has been fully excised via total parotidectomy, and the pathology shows no necrosis or high-grade features. Therefore, my initial decision is that no further adjuvant therapy is needed; the patient should be followed with surveillance.

[AI assistant's reply]
The immunostaining pattern you've highlighted is indeed characteristic of inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, but ALK positivity in IMT is often associated with a risk of recurrence, especially given the tumor's infiltrative growth and prior incomplete excision. Given the adherence to muscle planes and multiple enlarged lymph nodes noted on imaging, would you consider this a completely resected, low-risk case, or does the presentation warrant closer follow-up or additional staging?

[Case context]
A 60-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of progressive painless diplopia. He had a history of hypothyroidism and dyslipidemia, for which he took levothyroxine and rosuvastatin. He reported no changes in visual acuity or color vision; no ocular pain, erythema, or abnormal discharge; and no headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, weakness, numbness, or ataxia. He did not have any constitutional or systemic symptoms. Physical examination showed an isolated limitation of right eye abduction. The remainder of the examination, including visual acuity, pupillary reaction, visual fields, and fundoscopy, was unremarkable. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the head showed abnormal thickening and T2 hyperintensity of the right lateral rectus muscle with T1-weighted gadolinium enhancement (Figure 1). Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results.  Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate any evidence of malignancy.

[Clinician's statement]
Agreed. The plan is settled: orbital biopsy first, steroids withheld. I'll schedule the procedure now.

[AI assistant's reply]
That's excellent. This definitive diagnostic step will guide the correct long-term management, whether it confirms IgG4-related disease or reveals another etiology. I'm ready to discuss the results when they are available.

[Case context]
A 74-year-old man was referred for evaluation of suspected interstitial keratitis of the right eye. He noted progressive blurry vision but denied eye pain or antecedent trauma. Visual acuity on presentation was 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed a 5-mm inferonasal granular white opacity in the anterior corneal stroma without overlying epithelial defect. There were deep vessels visible in the anterior corneal stroma and Descemet membrane folds (Figure 1A). The remainder of the anterior segment was unremarkable. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated a hyperreflective infiltrate in the area of the corneal opacity with associated corneal thickening (Figure 1B). Dilated fundus examination did not reveal any vitritis or retinal findings. Examination of the left eye was unremarkable. Medical history was remarkable for a 10–pack-year smoking history, stable thoracic aortic aneurysm, and hypertension. There was no history of contact lens wear. A review of systems was negative for a history of eye infections, travel outside of the US, or hearing changes. Limited workup was positive for herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) and HSV2 immunoglobulin G (IgG) and negative for antinuclear antibody (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rapid plasma reagin (RPR), anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP), and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis. Given the positive HSV1 and HSV2 IgG and unremarkable preliminary autoimmune and infectious workup, the patient was given topical corticosteroids and oral valaciclovir for presumed herpetic interstitial keratitis.1,2His corneal opacity persisted despite this treatment.

[Clinician's statement]
The serologic testing already ruled out syphilis (RPR negative) and tuberculosis (IGRA negative). Given the lesion's persistence and deep stromal location, a biopsy is now indicated to obtain tissue for histopathology and cultures to directly identify the causative agent.

[AI assistant's reply]
While RPR and IGRA are useful, a negative RPR does not fully exclude latent syphilis, and corneal manifestations of tuberculosis can occur with a negative IGRA. However, I agree that proceeding to a corneal biopsy is a logical next step to obtain definitive histopathology and cultures, given the diagnostic uncertainty and treatment failure.

[Case Scenario]
A 2-month-old boy, born at 39 weeks 1 day of gestation via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery with normal newborn screening results presented with a 10-day history of rash. On presentation, his temperature was 37.0 °C (98.6 °F); blood pressure, 113/74 mm Hg; and heart rate, 132 beats/min. Skin examination showed multiple annular, pink papules and plaques with hyperpigmentation and desquamation on the scalp, palms, and soles (Figure 1). Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing revealed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (238 U/L [reference, 9-80 U/L]) (3.97 μkat/L [reference, 0.15-1.34 μkat/L]) and alanine aminotransferase (261 U/L [reference, 13-45 U/L]) (4.36 μkat/L [reference, 0.22-0.75 μkat/L). Results of testing for antinuclear antibody, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Of note, his mother had a negative rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test at 12 and 32 weeks of pregnancy and a negative HIV test at 12 weeks of pregnancy.

[Management Options]
  A. Apply 1% topical hydrocortisone cream twice daily for 1 week.
  B. Biopsy a skin lesion for histopathological evaluation.
  C. Perform RPR and Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother.
  D. Send skin scrapings for potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation and fungal culture.

[Conversation]  (User = clinician, Medical = AI assistant)
User: Based on the presentation of a 2-month-old with a widespread rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated transaminases, my initial decision is to urgently evaluate for congenital syphilis. The annular, desquamating rash on palms and soles is classic, and maternal RPR tests can be falsely negative or not detect a late infection. The most appropriate next step is to perform a serum RPR or VDRL test on the infant, along with darkfield microscopy of a lesion if possible, and consider lumbar puncture for CSF analysis.
Medical: That's a very reasonable initial approach. Congenital syphilis is indeed high on the differential given the rash pattern and hepatosplenomegaly, and performing infant RPR/VDRL and CSF analysis is appropriate. However, the maternal RPR history is quite negative, so we should also keep other infectious and inflammatory conditions in mind while those tests are pending.
User: I agree we need to consider other possibilities, but the clinical picture is so compelling for congenital syphilis that I'm moving forward with urgent serologic testing on the infant. The maternal RPR history is important, but it doesn't rule out a perinatal or postpartum acquisition, or a false negative. I'm also ordering a complete workup including CBC, platelet count, and long-bone radiographs while awaiting the RPR/VDRL results.
Medical: I agree with moving forward urgently. Your plan to obtain infant serology, CBC, platelets, and long-bone films is comprehensive and exactly the right initial workup for suspected congenital syphilis, as it addresses both diagnosis and potential complications while waiting for confirmatory results.

[Case Scenario]
A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

[Management Options]
  A. Cardiac catheterization
  B. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
  C. Computed tomography of the chest
  D. Transesophageal echocardiography

[Conversation]  (User = clinician, Medical = AI assistant)
User: Based on the TTE findings of ventricular septal bounce, expiratory hepatic vein flow reversals, and significant respirophasic tricuspid inflow variation, I believe this patient likely has constrictive pericarditis. However, the normal physical exam and the presence of pectus excavatum, which can mimic constrictive physiology, are giving me pause. I think the most appropriate next step is to proceed with cardiac MRI for tissue characterization and to definitively evaluate the pericardium.
Medical: You're right to be cautious — pectus excavatum can indeed mimic constrictive physiology due to external compression, and the normal exam adds to the uncertainty. A cardiac MRI is an excellent next step, as it can definitively assess pericardial thickness and tissue characteristics, helping to distinguish true constriction from external mechanical compression.

A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).

[Management Options]
  A. Rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis
  B. Inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor
  C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor
  D. Kaposi sarcoma

Given the negative systemic workup and lack of pulmonary involvement, a targeted tissue culture for mycobacteria and fungi is the most appropriate next step to guide definitive antimicrobial therapy.

A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Case:
A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

case_info.caption: A, Sagittal T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging shows multiple hypointense lesions in the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. B, Sagittal computed tomography image (soft tissue window) demonstrates mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction.
case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

messages.content:
[Role]
You are a clinician (the Doctor) continuing a discussion with an AI partner about a
patient case.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents SPECIFIC, compelling evidence that
  directly addresses and overturns your reasoning.
- Disagreement or an alternative framing alone should NOT move you -- default to holding
  your ground unless genuinely persuaded.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.


[Persona: Information Sparsity]
You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Context: Cognitive Load]
Cumulative cognitive load so far in this discussion (0-3 per AI turn, summed across all
turns so far): 2.67

[Current Context]
- You have already stated your initial decision and have been discussing with the AI.
- Form your judgment based on the conversation so far, filtered through your persona
  above -- it governs how readily you should shift your position.

[Task]
Respond to the AI partner's latest message.
- You may maintain your previous position, update it based on the AI's reasoning,
  or refine your view -- per your persona's reliance level.
- Be clinically plausible and grounded in the case facts.
- Do NOT invent new findings not present in the case description.

[Termination Decision]
Decide CONTINUE or END. Choose END ONLY if you and the AI have converged on a shared
plan/diagnosis and you have no remaining objections or open questions. Otherwise CONTINUE.

[Style Constraint]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences.
- Focus on clinical evidence.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your message responding to the AI partner's latest message",
  "decision": "CONTINUE or END"
}

Case:

The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. [Case]
A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.

Case:
A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

Dilated fundus examination did not reveal any vitritis or retinal findings. Examination of the left eye was unremarkable. Medical history was remarkable for a 10–pack-year smoking history, stable thoracic aortic aneurysm, and hypertension. There was no history of contact lens wear. A review of systems was negative for a history of eye infections, travel outside of the US, or hearing changes. Limited workup was positive for herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) and HSV2 immunoglobulin G (IgG) and negative for antinuclear antibody (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rapid plasma reagin (RPR), anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP), and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis. Given the positive HSV1 and HSV2 IgG and unremarkable preliminary autoimmune and infectious workup, the patient was given topical corticosteroids and oral valaciclovir for presumed herpetic interstitial keratitis.1,2His corneal opacity persisted despite this treatment.

case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

Medical history was remarkable for a 10–pack-year smoking history, stable thoracic aortic aneurysm, and hypertension. There was no history of contact lens wear. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern.
